title: Evaluation of Dauphin Island Power Plant
text:
Executive Summary
This report evaluates the risk that a coastal power plant near Dauphin Island, Alabama will be forced to operate at reduced capacity due to elevated gulf water temperatures. The plant relies on water from the gulf as a heat sink and has to reduce output when temperatures exceed 85°F. The goal of this analysis is to see how often this threshold is exceeded and whether these periods correlate with electricity demand.
Two publicly available datasets were analyzed in order to address this. Water temperature data from NOAA was used to find periods when temperatures exceed the threshold. Electricity demand data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) was used to examine when peak demand occurs. These datasets were cleaned, aligned by date, and summarized using descriptive statistics and visual analysis.
The results show that water temperatures above 85°F occur often during summer months. These periods overlap with increases in electricity demand, which are likely driven by cooling needs. This creates a situation where the plant may have to reduce output at the same time demand is highest.

title: Evaluation of Dauphin Island Power Plant
text:
Conclusion
The plant faces a strong risk of reduced operating capacity during high demand periods, especially in the summer. This overlap increases the likelihood of strain on the electrical system and reduces flexibility.

title: Evaluation of Dauphin Island Power Plant
text:
Recommendations

Evaluate possible other cooling strategies to reduce dependence on the gulf
Incorporate temperature risk into planning for future operations

Overall, this analysis indicates that rising water temperatures are a risk that should be accounted for in future planning and decision-making.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Electric power systems are very sensitive to environmental conditions, particularly temperature. Power plants that rely on nearby water bodies as heat sinks may have operational constraints when water temperatures rise above certain thresholds. As climate change continues, the risk of higher water temperatures becomes a concern.



Conceptual diagram of a coastal power plant cooling system. Seawater is drawn through intake pipes and used to remove heat from the plant.


Water temperature data from NOAA shows that temperatures vary seasonally and can become elevated during summer months (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 2026).
In addition, Electricity demand data from the EIA indicates increased demand during summer due to cooling needs (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2026). This overlap creates potential stress on power systems when both supply constraints and demand pressures happen simultaneously.
This study aims to assess the risk that a coastal power plant near Dauphin Island, Alabama will need to operate at reduced capacity. Specifically, it looks at the frequency and timing of high water temperature and compares these periods with patterns in regional electricity demand.
To address this question, data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 2026) and the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2026) are analyzed graphically to evaluate temperature and demand trends.




National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 2026. “NDBC Station Page.” https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/station_page.php?station=DPHA1.


U.S. Energy Information Administration. 2026. “Real-Time Operating Grid - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).” https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/index.php.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.1 Data Sources
Water temperature data was obtained from NOAA’s National Data Buoy Center station DPHA1 located near Dauphin Island, Alabama (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 2026). The dataset includes high-frequency observations of approximate 30-minute intervals of water temperature (WTMP), measured in degrees Celsius. These measurements are taken by buoy sensors near the ocean surface.
Electricity demand data was obtained from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA-930 dataset) (U.S. Energy Information Administration 2026), which provides hourly estimates of electricity demand (MW) for balancing authorities across the United States.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.2 Data Processing
Water temperature data was cleaned by removing missing values. Temperatures were converted from degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit to evaluate the 85°F operational threshold.
Electricity demand data from two EIA-930 datasets (January–June 2025 and July–December 2025) were combined to produce a full-year dataframe. Datetime variables were constructed using date and hour information, and rows with missing values were removed.
A small number of observations with missing temperature or demand values were removed, and extreme values by bounding observations between reasonable values (specifically 23-104°F water temperature only). These values were scattered minimally throughout the dataset and did not occur in continuous chunks. No interpolation was performed, and gaps in the data were not artificially connected in visualizations.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.3 Variable Construction
Water temperature observations were recorded at approximately 30-minute intervals. Daily maximum temperature (°F) was calculated to identify days exceeding the 85°F threshold.
Electricity demand was aggregated to daily average demand (MW) to align with temperature data.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.4 Analysis Approach
The primary analysis evaluated the frequency and duration of observations where water temperature exceeded 85°F.
The secondary analysis compared daily temperature and electricity demand by identifying days where temperature exceeded 85°F and examining how these periods aligned with demand patterns.
The results were visualized using time series plots and summary statistics.

U.S. Energy Information Administration. 2026. “Real-Time Operating Grid - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).” https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/index.php.

Table 3.1 summarizes key components of temperature and demand values. The summary statistics indicate that temperatures exceeding 85°F are not rare and occur frequently during the observed period. Maximum temperatures substantially exceed the operational threshold, indicating potential for sustained stress on cooling systems. Additionally, average electricity demand is higher on days exceeding 85°F compared to overall demand, suggesting that reduced cooling efficiency is likely to coincide with periods of elevated system load.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.3 Water Temperature Data
The water temperature dataset has frequent measurements of water temperature (WTMP) measured in degrees Celsius. After cleaning the data and removing missing values we are left with data spanning 2025, as shown in Figure 3.1. Water temperature values were converted from Celsius to Fahrenheit to correspond with the 85°F threshold.
The data shows that temperatures vary seasonally throughout the year. Lower temperatures occur during winter months and higher temperatures during summer. We see continuous examples of the water being above 85°F during the summer months.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.4 Electricity Demand Data
The electricity demand dataset is measured hourly, deriving electricity demand values measured in megawatts (MW). Demand levels vary throughout the day and across seasons, but higher values are observed during summer and winter months when heating and cooling are in demand.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.5 Primary Analysis
The primary analysis looks at instances of water temperatures exceeding 85°F. These values represent periods when Gulf water temperatures reach levels associated with higher heat conditions.
The analysis identifies the frequency and duration of observations where water temperature exceeds this threshold. This occurs mainly during summer months and appears in clusters of consecutive hours and days.
Figure 3.1 shows the time series of water temperature observations.








Figure 3.1: Daily maximum water temperature at Dauphin Island in 2025. The dashed line marks the 85°F operational threshold.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.6 Secondary Analysis
The secondary analysis examines electricity demand patterns during periods when water temperatures exceed 85°F.
Dates with water temperatures above 85°F were identified and overlaid on the electricity demand time series. Shaded regions in Figure 3.2 indicate days when water temperatures exceeded the 85°F threshold.








Figure 3.2: Daily maximum water temperature (top) and average electricity demand (bottom). Shaded regions indicate days when water temperature exceeded 85°F.





High water temperature days occur primarily during the summer portion of the electricity demand curve. Figure 3.2 shows that many of these days coincide with periods of higher electricity demand.
These results indicate that periods when water temperature exceeds 85°F often overlap with moderate to high electricity demand.

title: 4  Conclusion
text:
4.1 Limitations
This analysis evaluated the risk that a coastal power plant near Dauphin Island, Alabama, may have to operate at reduced capacity due to elevated Gulf water temperatures. Water temperature data from NOAA and electricity demand data from the EIA were used to identify periods where water temperature exceeded 85°F and compare those periods to electricity demand.
The results show that water temperatures above 85°F occur primarily during summer months and often remain over 85 degrees for several consecutive days. These high-temperature periods overlap with higher electricity demand, which is likely driven by increased cooling needs. This overlap creates conditions where the plant may be required to reduce output at the same time electricity demand is high.
These findings suggest an operational risk during peak summer conditions. Reduced generating capacity during periods of elevated demand could increase system strain.
This analysis is subject to several limitations. It assumes that the 85°F threshold is fixed and doesn’t account for potential operational changes within the plant. Also, the demand data represents regional averages rather than being specific to the plant.
This analysis is limited to data from 2025, which may not fully capture long-term variability in water temperature or electricity demand. Multi-year analysis would provide a sounder estimate of risk, but the 2025 data is sufficient to illustrate seasonal patterns and potential operational concerns.
Despite these limitations, the analysis provides reasonable information for planning. The results indicate that high-temperature risk is seasonal and predictable, allowing mitigation to be performed during summer months.

title: 4  Conclusion
text:
ImportantExecutive Takeaways




Water temperatures above 85°F occur regularly during summer months

These periods overlap with higher electricity demand

Reduced plant capacity is most likely during peak summer demand

Seasonal mitigation strategies could reduce operational risk





Explore alternative cooling strategies, such as drawing cooler water from deeper or alternative intake locations

Plan operations around seasonal risk by scheduling maintenance outside peak summer months

Implement demand management strategies during extreme heat events to reduce system strain
